subject: Cognitive Science
title: Stereotypes as Categories
description: A fast breakdown of Stereotypes as Categories for builders.

hook.text: You assume the tall man plays basketball. That snap judgment used a social category—a stereotype.

buildup.text: Stereotypes are prototypes applied to people: expected traits mapped onto group membership.

discovery.text: They activate automatically. In milliseconds, category cues trigger trait associations.

twist.text: Even people who reject a stereotype show its activation in implicit association tests.

climax.text: The same mechanism that helps you quickly spot a chair also makes you prejudge a stranger.

quiz.question: How do stereotypes relate to categorization?
options: They apply prototype-like expectations to social groups

details.summary: Stereotypes are categories applied to social groups, with the same cognitive structures as any other category: prototypes, typicality effects, and essentialist assumptions.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding stereotypes as ordinary categories explains their persistence. They are not character flaws but products of the same cognitive processes that enable all categorization.
takeaways: Stereotypes follow the same rules as other categories
They activate automatically and influence judgment
Categorical efficiency makes stereotypes resistant to change

faq.question: Why are stereotypes so hard to change?
faq.answer: Stereotypes are maintained by confirmation bias, where people notice confirming evidence and ignore disconfirming evidence. A counter-stereotypic individual may be seen as an exception rather than a reason to update the category. Categories resist change because stability is their purpose.

faq.question: Can stereotypes be activated without awareness?
faq.answer: Yes. Implicit association tests show that people respond faster when stereotypic pairings are congruent. Even people who consciously reject stereotypes show automatic activation. Awareness of this automaticity is important because it affects behavior in split-second decisions.
